chunks: From him, from Abu Ali ibn Ayyub, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Abdullah ibn Bukayr, from Abdullah al-Lahham, who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who buys the daughter of a man from the People of Polytheism and takes her as a slave, and he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

And this does not contradict what was narrated - Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Sahl from Zakariyya ibn Adam, who said: I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about a man from the People of the Covenant (Ahl al-Dhimma) who was struck by famine, and a man brought his child to him and said, 'This is for you; feed him, and he is your slave.' He said, 'A free person is not bought, for he is not suitable for you, nor [is he] from the People of the Covenant.'

Because this report is specific to those who are from the People of the Covenant, because they do not deserve captivity due to their submission to the Jizya, and the first report covers those who were in the Land of War, and there is no contradiction between them in any case.
ai.seo_question: Can a Muslim buy a slave from the People of the Covenant (Ahl al-Dhimma) or polytheists?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi reconciles the apparent contradiction between the permissibility of purchasing a polytheist's daughter and the prohibition of buying a free child from the People of the Covenant by distinguishing their legal statuses: the former belongs to Dar al-Harb (land of war) where captivity applies, while the latter are exempt from sabiy due to their Jizya status. This distinction highlights the nuanced Shia jurisprudence regarding the acquisition of slaves from non-Muslims based on their political and fiscal relationship with the Islamic state.
